_comment: Executable test cases, one group per concept in misconceptions.csv.
Each group contains at least one case chosen specifically to fail on
that concept's misconception and pass on a correct implementation --
the `rationale` field says which one that is and why. The remaining
cases are ordinary correctness checks so a fix that breaks something
else does not read as a success.
`call` is evaluated in the namespace the student's code defines, so a
case can exercise a class or a sqlite3 connection, not only a plain
function. Tuples are normalised to lists in the call expression where
needed, because the expected values come from JSON and JSON has no

cases.name: target at the first position
cases.rationale: Passes even with the bug. Present so a fix cannot be claimed from this case alone.

cases.name: target at the last position
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: returning False inside the loop gives up after index 0.

cases.name: target absent
cases.rationale: A fix that always returns True would pass the first two cases.

cases.name: empty list
cases.rationale: Boundary: no iterations at all.

cases.name: target in the middle
cases.rationale: Found on the first probe, so it passes with the bug present.

cases.name: absent target terminates
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: with high = mid the window stops shrinking once it holds two elements and the loop never ends. Isolated so the hang does not take the batch with it.

cases.name: first element
cases.rationale: Drives the window down to the low end, where the off-by-one shows.

cases.name: last element
cases.rationale: Drives the window to the high end.

cases.name: single-element list
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: with while low < high and low == high == 0 the body never runs, so the only candidate is never compared.

cases.name: last element
cases.rationale: The search narrows to a single remaining candidate, which the strict comparison skips.

cases.name: target in the middle
cases.rationale: Ordinary case; passes with the bug.

cases.name: absent target
cases.rationale: A fix that returns low instead of -1 would fail here.

cases.name: unsorted input returns the original index
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: sorting a copy puts 10 at index 0, but in the caller's list it is at index 1.

cases.name: already-sorted input
cases.rationale: Passes with the bug, because sorting changes nothing here.

cases.name: input is not modified
cases.rationale: Sorting the caller's list in place rather than a copy is the other half of this mistake.

cases.name: absent target
cases.rationale: Boundary.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Correctness. Passes with the bug, which costs time rather than accuracy.

cases.name: already-sorted input exits early
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception. On 40 already-sorted elements one pass reads about 80 times; without the swapped flag it reads about 3100. The returned list is identical either way, so this is the only way to see the difference.

cases.name: reversed input
cases.rationale: Worst case: the early exit must not fire before the list is actually sorted.

cases.name: duplicates
cases.rationale: Equal elements must not be treated as needing a swap, which would stop the early exit ever firing.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Correctness. Swapping inside the inner loop still sorts, so this passes with the bug.

cases.name: one swap per outer pass
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception. Selection sort makes at most n-1 swaps, so about 38 writes for 20 elements; swapping during every comparison instead makes roughly 190 swaps and 380 writes. Both produce the same sorted list.

cases.name: already sorted
cases.rationale: Must not disturb an ordered list.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: shifting without saving the key overwrites it, so an element is duplicated and another lost.

cases.name: reversed input
cases.rationale: Every element shifts the full distance, which is where an off-by-one in the insert position shows.

cases.name: no elements are lost
cases.rationale: The shifting bug duplicates values. Comparing the multiset catches that even if the order happens to look right.

cases.name: single element
cases.rationale: Boundary: the inner loop never runs.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Correctness. This misconception is about memory, not output, so no value case can catch it -- see the in-place case below.

cases.name: sorts in place rather than returning a fresh list
cases.rationale: Catches what is catchable: an implementation built on arr[:mid] slices returns a new list and leaves the caller's list untouched, so the second element of this pair stays unsorted.

cases.name: duplicates are kept
cases.rationale: Merging must not drop equal elements.

cases.name: interleaved halves
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: if the sub-array pointer never advances, the same element is written repeatedly and the merge either loops forever or fills the output with one value.

cases.name: no elements are lost or duplicated
cases.rationale: Duplicate writes show up as a changed multiset even when the result is ordered.

cases.name: already sorted
cases.rationale: One side exhausts first, which is where the tail copy is usually wrong.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: including the pivot in both halves means a sub-array never shrinks, so the recursion repeats until Python raises RecursionError.

cases.name: already-sorted input
cases.rationale: The worst case for a last-element pivot, and the fastest way to exhaust the stack if the bounds are wrong.

cases.name: two elements
cases.rationale: The smallest input where a sub-array can fail to shrink.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: swapping before advancing the boundary leaves an element on the wrong side of the pivot.

cases.name: duplicates
cases.rationale: Equal elements are where an off-by-one boundary most often misplaces a value.

cases.name: reversed input
cases.rationale: Every element crosses the boundary.

cases.name: three already-sorted elements
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception. With left = 2*i the root's left child is the root itself, so index 0 is never compared against its real children and the last two elements come back swapped. This is the smallest input that distinguishes the two: most larger inputs happen to sort correctly anyway.

cases.name: sorts a shuffled list
cases.rationale: Correctness. Passes with the bug: 1-indexed child arithmetic still sorts about 80% of random inputs, which is why this misconception survives casual testing.

cases.name: index arithmetic stays in range
cases.rationale: A longer input exercises deeper levels of the heap, where the wrong child index addresses a node outside the sub-heap being sifted.

cases.name: duplicates
cases.rationale: Sift-down must handle equal keys without looping.

cases.name: diamond graph visits each vertex once
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: D is reachable from both B and C, so marking visited at dequeue rather than enqueue puts D on the queue twice and reports it twice.

cases.name: a cycle does not loop forever
cases.rationale: No visited tracking at all turns a cycle into an infinite traversal.

cases.name: breadth-first order is preserved
cases.rationale: A fix that switches to a stack would pass the duplicate check and fail here.

cases.name: isolated start vertex
cases.rationale: Boundary: no neighbours.

cases.name: diamond DAG is not a cycle
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: D is reached twice by different paths, and treating any revisit as a cycle reports this acyclic graph as cyclic.

cases.name: a real cycle is found
cases.rationale: A fix that always returns False would pass the first case.

cases.name: self loop
cases.rationale: The shortest possible cycle; often missed when the stack check happens before the vertex is pushed.

cases.name: empty graph
cases.rationale: Boundary.

cases.name: factorial of zero
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: a base case of n == 1 is stepped straight past by n == 0, and the recursion runs until Python raises RecursionError.

cases.name: factorial of one
cases.rationale: Passes with the bug, since n == 1 is exactly the case the wrong base case handles.

cases.name: factorial of five
cases.rationale: Ordinary case; also passes with the bug.

cases.name: adjacent matches are all removed
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: removing while iterating shifts the list under the iterator, so the second 2 is skipped and survives.

cases.name: every element matches
cases.rationale: The skip happens on every step, so roughly half the elements remain.

cases.name: the caller's list is unchanged
cases.rationale: Mutating the argument is the other half of this mistake.

cases.name: value not present
cases.rationale: Boundary: nothing to remove.

cases.name: a later call starts from an empty bucket
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: a mutable default is created once at definition time, so the second call returns [1, 2].

cases.name: the first call looks correct
cases.rationale: The bug is invisible on a single call, which is why it survives review.

cases.name: three calls stay independent
cases.rationale: Accumulation compounds, so the third call is unambiguous.

cases.name: an explicit bucket is appended to
cases.rationale: A fix that ignores the parameter and always starts fresh would fail here.

cases.name: the caller's list is unchanged
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: binding the argument to another name does not copy it, so appending is visible through the caller's reference.

cases.name: the returned list is correct
cases.rationale: Passes with the bug, because the return value is right either way.

cases.name: two calls do not accumulate
cases.rationale: If the first call mutated src, the second returns [1, 2, 3].

cases.name: empty input
cases.rationale: Boundary.

cases.name: colliding keys are both kept
cases.call: [[list(p) for p in b] for b in build_index([(1, 'a'), (3, 'b')], 2)]
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: 1 and 3 both hash to bucket 1, and overwriting instead of chaining loses the first pair. Integer keys are used because string hashing is randomised per process.

cases.name: keys in different buckets
cases.call: [[list(p) for p in b] for b in build_index([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')], 2)]
cases.rationale: Passes with the bug, since nothing collides.

cases.name: insertion order within a bucket
cases.call: [[list(p) for p in b] for b in build_index([(5, 'x'), (1, 'y'), (3, 'z')], 2)]
cases.rationale: Three-way collision; a fix that prepends instead of appending would fail here.

cases.name: empty input
cases.rationale: Boundary: the table must still be the requested size.

cases.name: a customer with no qualifying orders still appears
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Ben'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,150),(2,1,200),(3,2,50);")
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: Ben's only order is 50, so filtering amount > 100 in WHERE removes his NULL-extended row entirely and he vanishes from the result. In the ON clause he survives with a total of 0.

cases.name: a customer with no orders at all
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Cara'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,500);")
cases.rationale: The plain LEFT JOIN case: no matching row at all, so the total must come from COALESCE rather than NULL.

cases.name: ordered by name
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Zoe'),(2,'Abe'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,200),(2,2,300);")
cases.rationale: The contract specifies an order, so the result must not depend on insertion order.

cases.name: many small orders exceed the threshold together
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Ben'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,50),(2,1,50),(3,1,50),(4,2,200);")
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: Ana's largest single order is 50, so a WHERE amount > 100 filter drops her even though her total is 150. HAVING runs after grouping and keeps her.

cases.name: a customer below the threshold is excluded
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Ben'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,300),(2,2,40);")
cases.rationale: A fix that drops the filter altogether would return Ben too.

cases.name: exactly at the threshold is excluded
cases.setup:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
conn.executescript("CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,100);")
cases.rationale: The contract says exceeds, so >= would be wrong.

cases.name: two baskets do not share contents
cases.rationale: Catches the misconception: a list defined at class level is created once and shared, so the apple appears in both baskets.

cases.name: one basket accumulates its own items
cases.rationale: Passes with the bug, which is why a single-instance test misses it.

cases.name: a fresh basket is empty
cases.rationale: Constructing the second basket after the first has been used is the ordering that makes the shared state obvious.
